..(Saturday through Thursday)
Issued at 409 PM EDT THU AUG 13 2026

The long term period will open amidst building upper level 
ridging in the southeastern CONUS, while upper level troughing 
will sit over the Northeast. At the surface, a weak warm front 
will be lifting northward. Southwesterly to westerly winds on the 
warm side of this boundary will help to maintain a highly moist 
environment; LREF mean PW values range from 2 inches in the 
northeastern forecast area to around 1.8 inches in the southwest, 
representing climatologically anomalous moisture generally 
exceeding the 90th percentile. Despite ridging attempting to build
in, eastern Kentucky will still find itself on the periphery of 
this feature. This could allow for additional convective activity 
to affect the eastern portion of the forecast area. Given moist 
antecedent conditions and a very favorable environment for 
torrential rainfall, any sustained convection could be capable of 
producing flash flooding, with a Marginal (Level 1/4) Risk for 
Excessive Rainfall in place across the majority of the forecast 
area. Furthermore, given ample moisture and increasingly warm 
temperatures, apparent temperatures should soar into the upper 90s
or perhaps low triple digits at their peak. As an additional 
consequence of this heat and humidity, a highly unstable 
environment is expected to build on Saturday afternoon. LREF 
output suggests mean MUCAPE of over 3000 J/kg; this would be more 
than enough instability to support strong or perhaps severe 
convection should storms initiate, although very weak shear in the
range of 10 to 20 kts should limit the threat of highly organized
and long-lived convection. For now, given weak forcing and the 
expectation of height rises, PoPs in the range of 20-30% have been
maintained for the eastern portions of the forecast area, with 
lower rain chances in our southwest where ridging influence will 
be the strongest. That being said, should convection initiate, 
isolated damaging wind gusts will be possible. Thus, the Storm 
Prediction Center has introduced a Marginal (Level 1/5) Risk for 
severe thunderstorms for most of the area on Saturday (excluding 
our southwestern counties). Regardless, any convection should 
cease with the loss of daytime heating.

Sunday should bring drier weather, although things wont stay dry 
for long. Additional ridging building aloft will make Sunday the 
hottest day of the week, with highs reaching the low to mid 90s 
across the forecast area. Given continued humidity, more 
widespread triple digit apparent temperatures may be possible 
Sunday afternoon; current LREF output suggests over a 30 percent 
chance of exceeding a 100 degree apparent temperature for the 
northern portions of our forecast area by only 2 PM on Sunday. 
Thankfully, this heat will be short lived. Additional upper level 
troughing will be digging into the Great Lakes region by Sunday 
afternoon, and a shortwave rotating through the base of this 
trough should work to flatten the upper level ridge somewhat by 
Sunday night. Meanwhile, a surface low will be located near 
Michigan, with a cold front extending to the southwest. As the 
system translates eastward, this front will approach Kentucky by 
early Monday morning, bringing the next round of rain. As in 
previous days, moisture will be quite high (with westerly flow 
supporting PW values generally in the range of 1.8-1.9 inches, 
approximately the 90th percentile), and at least isolated 
instances of flash flooding will be possible. Thus, WPC has placed
the northern and eastern portions of the forecast area in a 
Marginal (Level 1/4) Risk for Excessive Rainfall on Monday. The 
magnitude of the flash flood risk will remain fairly dependent on 
how saturated soils are going into the event, in addition to the 
timing of this frontal passage (which itself will modulate how 
widespread any convection is); therefore, uncertainty remains 
high. Regardless, rain appears likely on Monday.

Following the frontal passage, temperatures will be much more
tolerable. With less influence from the upper level ridge, MaxTs
will generally range from the mid to upper 80s across the forecast
area, with the hottest temperatures expected to the southwest.
Moisture will be noticeably lower too, with dewpoints generally
falling into the upper 60s across the forecast area. That being
said, the general pattern will still be fairly active. Upper level
troughing over the Great Lakes will persist, while ridging will
dominate across the southern CONUS, with models generally
depicting the ridge axis in the Four Corners region or slightly
farther east in western Texas. This will place eastern Kentucky in
a region of either quasi zonal or northwest flow aloft, depending
on which model you believe; either way, this will open the door
for additional rain chances through the end of the period.
